newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia high aromatic naphtha surplus weighs on price.
newsitem.headline: Asia high aromatic naphtha surplus weighs on price.

text.p: High aromatic naphtha (HAN) prices in Asia are under pressure amid low demand for the gasoline feedstock, traders said on Tuesday.
The naphtha, also known as high naphthenic and aromatic (N+A), is cracked to produce benzene, toluene and xylene -- components used both for gasoline blending and in petrochemical manufacturing.
Heavy maintenance schedules at South Korean and Japanese refineries -- major HAN buyers -- in May and June, have depressed demand.
Light distillate stocks in Singapore are high and gasoline prices have fallen, reflecting the weakness of the market.
The weakness of the HAN market emerged earlier this month when Indian cancelled a tender to sell the product from Cochin April 30-May 2 because it considered all the bids too low, trade sources said.

IOC reoffered the product and finally accepted a record low bid. It sold 30,000 tonnes of HAN around $40 per tonne below Japanese spot quotes, for May 6-7 lifting free-on-board (fob) Cochin on the west coast.
Traders said the price was a record low for India, which last year sold similar cargoes at $16-$20 discount. IOC's last HAN award, for April 1-3 lifting from Cochin at a discount of $19.08.
"I am not surprised at the huge discount," said one feedstock buyer on the award. "The typical destination for this cargo is Japan and South Korea...but N+A is a bit on the long side until July."
The weak market has seen gasoline prices in Singapore plunge to less than $24.00 per barrel, from $29.00 in mid-March.
Light distillate stocks in Singapore are near two-year highs around 7.5 million barrels. Traders said they estimated most of the light distillate was gasoline.
Refiner Ssangyong Oil added to Asia's gasoline supplies earlier this month, after starting its 40,000-barrel-per-day (bpd) residue fluid catalytic cracker.
South Korea was now an exporter of gasoline to the tune of 50,000 bpd, traders said.
"Traditionally N+A is traded at a premium to the lighter naphtha grade as there are limited supplies and most refiners use N+A to reform into gasoline," a trader said.
Regional N+A supplies can typically only be found in limited volumes from Australia, Indonesia, India and Malaysia, he said.
"But I don't see much of a premium as mogas is weak," he said, referrring to the premium over light naphtha.
